extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical researchers, and advanced students interested in research problems, foundations, and methods
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for selecting, posing, and judging mathematical research problems and their solutions; covers desiderata for a 'good' problem, methodological advice, and formal requirements for correctness and rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and ease of comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical problem should be clear and easily comprehended; clearness and ease of comprehension attract while the complicated repels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert quotes an old French maxim about making a theory explainable to a passerby and insists this clearness is even more desirable for a problem. A clear statement attracts solvers and increases the problem's appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate difficulty (enticing but accessible)
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem should be difficult enough to entice but not completely inaccessible, so it does not mock our efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The problem should serve as a guide post on paths to hidden truths and provide pleasure in successful solution; examples include classical hard-but-productive problems (brachistochrone, Fermat's last theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / usefulness for advancement of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A good problem has deep significance for the advance of mathematical science and plays an important role in the work of the individual investigator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert cites examples (Fermat's problem led to ideal numbers; three-body problem led to new celestial mechanics methods) to show that important problems stimulate new theories and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertility: leads to new methods and wider theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem is valuable if working on it leads to new methods, outlooks, or branches of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bernoulli's brachistochrone leading to calculus of variations; Fermat's problem prompting Kummer's ideals and generalizations in algebra and function theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad applicability across branches
rubrics_metrics.description: A single special problem may find application in widely different branches of mathematical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes the shortest line problem is central in geometry, calculus of variations, mechanics; Klein's work on icosahedron connects regular polyhedra to group theory and differential equations—this breadth increases a problem's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact formulation of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem statements must include a finite number of hypotheses which are implied in the statement and must always be exactly formulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert emphasizes that correctness must be established from explicitly stated hypotheses; vagueness in hypotheses undermines the possibility of rigorous proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of rigor: finite logical deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution should be verifiable by a finite number of logical steps based on the finite hypotheses of the problem (the requirement of rigor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor is necessary for a perfect solution; Hilbert argues rigor often leads to simpler, more general methods and is philosophically required for mathematical certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor promotes simplicity and generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor in proof is not the enemy of simplicity; the effort for rigor tends to find simpler proofs and more developable methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert gives examples (function-theoretical methods simplifying algebraic curve theory; Weierstrass's work in calculus of variations) showing rigor can simplify and unify theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of geometric/diagrammatic reasoning only with axiomatic grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of geometrical signs and figures as means of proof presupposes exact knowledge and mastery of the axioms underlying those figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometrical pictures are mnemonic but must be incorporated into the general treasure of mathematical signs only after rigorous axiomatic investigation; axioms determine correct use of diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate introduction and justification of new concepts and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: New concepts should be investigated and fixed by axioms, and new signs chosen to remind one of the originating phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes that new mathematical ideas require axiomatic foundation and that new symbols should serve as mnemonic ties to their motivating phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek general standpoints / generalization before ad-hoc methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure often stems from not recognizing the more general standpoint from which the problem is only a link in a chain; finding this standpoint yields methods applicable to related problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cauchy's complex integration methods, Kummer's ideals - general methods are the most practicable and certain way to advance on problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialization and solve simpler problems (laddering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialization—finding and solving simpler, related problems—is often more productive than seeking immediate general methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert advises identifying easier subproblems and solving them with devices as perfect as possible; this is a key lever for overcoming difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider impossibility proofs as valid and valuable outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: If a solution is impossible under given hypotheses, proving that impossibility is a legitimate and important result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: impossibility proofs led to satisfactory resolution of parallel postulate, squaring the circle, solution of quintic by radicals; impossibility proofs can redirect or clarify the sense of problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical conviction of decidability (solvability or impossibility by finite reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert asserts a conviction (axiom) that every definite mathematical problem admits exact settlement either by solution or by proof of impossibility via finite logical processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'no ignorabimus' attitude is presented as a motivational principle for mathematical work; it's a criterion shaping the expectation of problems' resolvability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate axioms: compatibility/consistency and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: In foundational problems, prove whether axioms are compatible (non-contradictory) and whether certain statements depend on other axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert describes proving compatibility as central: constructing models to show non-contradiction and isolating dependent parts of axiomatic systems; proving compatibility demonstrates mathematical existence of systems (e.g., the continuum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit counterexamples or demonstrate non-decomposability when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: To show impossibility of certain decompositional proofs, one should specify explicit constructions (e.g., tetrahedra of equal base and altitude that cannot be split into congruent tetrahedra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert suggests explicit counterexamples can settle impossibility questions in geometry and solid figures; he cites the Euclidean tetrahedra volume problem as an instance where exhibiting concrete examples proves impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze which axioms are necessary for particular theorems (axiomatic minimality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether specific theorems (e.g., 'straight line is shortest between two points') require which congruence axioms, and construct geometries with selected axioms satisfied or violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert develops the idea of geometries 'next to' Euclidean by tweaking which axioms hold, to understand the logical dependencies of familiar theorems and the idea of distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question and minimize auxiliary assumptions (e.g., differentiability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether commonly assumed properties (like differentiability in Lie's theory) are truly necessary or can be derived from other concepts/axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert raises the question whether Lie's differentiability assumption is avoidable or whether groups can be transformed into ones with differentiable defining functions; this encourages scrutiny of hidden or heavy hypotheses in theories and functional equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize technical necessary and sufficient conditions in specialized areas (calculus of variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In problems about extrema (calculus of variations), apply the necessary and sufficient analytic conditions (e.g., Jacobi's condition together with Weierstrass's E > 0) to judge minima.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert outlines that, for variational problems, vanishing of first variation plus Jacobi and Weierstrass conditions form the analytic framework to decide minima; related integral identities and polar processes are tools to derive these conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate functional-equation and analytic techniques without unwarranted smoothness assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating functional equations and difference equations, attempt to derive differentiability or other regularity from the equation itself rather than assuming it a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert cites Minkowski and examples of analytic functional equations whose sole solutions may be nowhere differentiable; he suggests studying such equations under weaker regularity hypotheses to broaden applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value cross-fertilization between theory and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems may originate from external experience or arise internally by logical combination; the interplay between thought and experience often yields analogies and links across branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert stresses that both empirical and internally-generated problems are valuable and that the interaction explains recurring analogies and harmony across mathematical disciplines.
